outcomes.text: Use rulers and measuring cylinders to measure lengths and volumes.
Define speed as distance divided by time and use the speed equation.
State that mass measures the amount of matter in an object.
Define density as mass per volume and use ρ = m/V.
Recognise that forces can alter an object's size or shape.
Describe moments as turning effects and give everyday examples.
State the meaning of centre of gravity.
Recognise that forces can alter an object's size or shape.
Construct and interpret load–extension graphs for elastic materials, including the related experiment.
Find the resultant of collinear forces.
State that motion remains stationary or uniform and straight unless a resultant force acts.
Explain that a resultant force can alter velocity by changing speed or direction.
Describe solid friction as a force opposing motion and causing heating.
Know that drag acts on objects moving through liquids.
Know that drag acts on objects moving through gases, including air resistance.
Calculate spring constant as force divided by extension.
Define the limit of proportionality and locate it on a load–extension graph.
Use F = ma and recognise that force and acceleration have the same direction.
Explain qualitatively how perpendicular force affects circular motion when speed, mass or radius changes.
Describe moments as turning effects of forces and identify everyday examples.
Calculate a moment using force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Apply the principle of moments to balanced beams and cases with one force on each side.
State that equilibrium requires both zero resultant force and zero resultant moment.
Apply the principle of moments when multiple forces act on either side of the pivot.
Describe an experiment showing that an equilibrium object has no resultant moment.
State the meaning of centre of gravity.
Describe an experiment for locating the centre of gravity of an irregular plane lamina.
Explain how centre-of-gravity position affects the stability of simple objects.
Produce and interpret load–extension graphs for elastic solids, including the related experimental method.
Find the resultant of forces acting along one straight line.
State Newton's first-law behaviour when no resultant force acts.
Explain that a resultant force changes velocity by altering speed, direction, or both.
Describe solid friction as a force that resists motion and generates heat.
Use F = ma, recognising that force and acceleration have the same direction.
Describe how force, mass, speed, and radius affect circular motion qualitatively.
Describe a force's moment as its turning effect and give everyday examples.
Calculate moment as force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Apply the principle of moments to balanced beams with one force on each side.
State that zero resultant force and moment indicate equilibrium.
Apply the principle of moments when multiple forces act on either side of a pivot.
Describe how to locate the centre of gravity of an irregular plane lamina experimentally.
Explain qualitatively how centre-of-gravity position affects the stability of simple objects.
Define momentum as mass times velocity and use p = mv.
Understand energy stores and transfers, mechanical work, energy resources, conservation, efficiency, and relationships involving kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and power.
Identify kinetic, gravitational, chemical, elastic, nuclear, electrostatic and thermal energy stores.
Understand that mechanical or electrical work equals transferred energy.
Describe how different renewable and non-renewable resources provide useful energy or electricity.
Define power as work done or energy transferred per unit time and use both equations.
Define pressure as force per area and use p = F/A.
Describe distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Describe particle arrangements, separations and motions in solids, liquids and gases, using diagrams.
Explain qualitatively how gas pressure responds to temperature or volume changes under stated conditions.
Identify the distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Name the changes of state between solids, liquids and gases, excluding gas-to-solid and solid-to-gas changes.
Describe and diagram particle arrangements, separations and movements in solids, liquids and gases.
Relate particle motion to temperature, including absolute zero at −273 °C, where kinetic energy is lowest.
Explain gas pressure and pressure changes using particle motion and collisions with surfaces.
Recognise random microscopic motion in suspensions as evidence for the kinetic particle model.
Explain Brownian motion as random collisions between suspended particles and surrounding gas or liquid particles.
Relate material properties to forces, separations and motions between atoms, molecules, ions and electrons.
Explain gas pressure changes as forces from particle collisions produce force per unit area.
Explain how collisions with rapidly moving molecules can move microscopic particles, distinguishing atoms and molecules from those particles.
Describe particle-level effects on fixed-mass gas pressure when temperature changes at constant volume or volume changes at constant temperature.
Convert between kelvin and Celsius temperatures using T = θ + 273.
Use pV = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, including graphical representations.
Know the distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Know the terms for changes of state between solids, liquids and gases, excluding gas–solid and solid–gas changes.
Describe particle arrangement, separation and movement in solids, liquids and gases, and represent them with simple diagrams.
Relate particle motion to temperature, including absolute zero at −273 °C, where particles have minimum kinetic energy.
Explain gas pressure and pressure changes using particle motion and collisions with surfaces.
Recognise random microscopic motion in suspensions as evidence supporting the kinetic particle model.
Explain Brownian motion as random collisions between suspended microscopic particles and surrounding gas or liquid particles.
Understand that interparticle forces, separations and motion determine the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Explain gas pressure and its changes using forces from particles colliding with surfaces, producing force per unit area.
Understand that collisions with rapidly moving molecules can move microscopic particles, distinguishing atoms and molecules from microscopic particles.
Describe how changing temperature at constant volume or volume at constant temperature affects fixed-mass gas pressure.
Convert between kelvin and Celsius using T = θ + 273, with temperature in kelvin and Celsius respectively.
Use pV = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, including graphical representations.
Describe how solids, liquids and gases expand when heated at constant pressure.
Give everyday uses and effects of thermal expansion.
Explain why solids, liquids and gases expand by different amounts using particle motion and arrangement.
Know that heating an object increases its internal energy.
Explain increased temperature as greater average kinetic energy of the particles.
Define specific heat capacity and use ΔE = mcΔθ.
Describe experiments measuring the specific heat capacity of solids and liquids.
Explain melting and boiling as energy input without temperature change.
State the melting and boiling temperatures of water at standard atmospheric pressure.
Describe condensation and solidification using particle ideas.
Explain evaporation as higher-energy particles escaping from a liquid surface.
Know that evaporation cools a liquid.
Distinguish boiling from evaporation.
Explain how temperature, surface area and air movement affect evaporation.
Explain cooling when an object contacts an evaporating liquid.
Understand how temperature affects matter and how thermal energy is transferred and stored.
Describe thermal expansion in solids, liquids and gases, compare their expansion, and explain practical applications and effects.
Relate temperature increases to internal energy, define and calculate specific heat capacity, and describe measurement experiments.
Explain melting, boiling, condensation, solidification and evaporation, including temperature conditions, particle behaviour and cooling effects.
Describe experiments comparing good and poor thermal conductors.
Explain conduction in solids through lattice vibrations and free-electron movement in metals.
Explain why gases and most liquids conduct thermal energy poorly using particle ideas.
Recognise that some solids conduct better than insulators but worse than good conductors.
Know that convection transfers thermal energy importantly in liquids and gases.
Explain convection through density changes and describe illustrative experiments.
Know that thermal radiation is infrared and is emitted by all objects.
Know that thermal radiation transfers energy without needing a medium.
Describe how surface colour and texture affect infrared emission, absorption and reflection.
Know that constant temperature requires equal rates of energy transfer in and out.
Predict temperature changes when incoming and outgoing energy-transfer rates differ.
Explain how Earth’s temperature depends on the balance of incoming and emitted radiation.
Describe experiments comparing infrared emitters.
Describe experiments comparing infrared absorbers.
Describe how radiation emission rate depends on surface temperature and area.
Explain everyday applications of conduction, convection and radiation, including pans and room heating.
Explain complex applications involving multiple transfer methods, including fires and car radiators.
Understand the ways thermal energy moves between objects or regions.
Understand thermal energy transfer through materials by conduction.
Understand thermal energy transfer in liquids and gases by convection.
Understand thermal energy transfer by infrared radiation.
Explain everyday and complex applications of conduction, convection and radiation, including heating pans, room heating, fires and car radiators.
Know that waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
Describe wave motion using ropes, springs and water-wave experiments.
Describe wavefront, wavelength, frequency, crest, trough, amplitude and speed.
Use v = fλ to calculate wave speed.
Describe transverse waves and identify electromagnetic, water and seismic S-waves as examples.
Describe longitudinal waves and identify sound and seismic P-waves as examples.
Describe reflection, refraction and diffraction of waves.
Use a ripple tank to demonstrate reflection, refraction and diffraction.
Explain how wavelength and gap width affect diffraction through a gap.
Explain how wavelength affects diffraction at an edge.
Understand wave energy transfer, wave motion, wave features and speed, transverse and longitudinal waves, reflection, refraction and diffraction.
Define and use normal, incidence angle and reflection angle.
Describe a plane-mirror image as virtual, same-sized and equally distant behind the mirror.
Apply the law that incidence angle equals reflection angle.
Construct, measure and calculate simple plane-mirror reflections.
Define and use normal, incidence angle and refraction angle.
Describe an experiment demonstrating refraction through transparent blocks.
Describe light crossing boundaries between two transparent media.
State the meaning of critical angle.
Describe internal and total internal reflection experimentally and in applications.
Define refractive index as a ratio of wave speeds in two regions.
Use n = sin i / sin r.
Use n = 1 / sin c.
Describe optical-fibre applications, especially telecommunications.
Describe converging and diverging thin lenses acting on parallel light.
Define focal length, principal axis and principal focus.
Draw and use ray diagrams for real images formed by converging lenses.
Describe images as enlarged, equal-sized or diminished; upright or inverted; real or virtual.
Explain that extrapolated diverging rays form a virtual image that cannot project onto a screen.
Draw and use ray diagrams for virtual images formed by converging lenses.
Describe how a single lens acts as a magnifying glass.
Explain lens correction of long-sightedness and short-sightedness.
Describe dispersion of white light by refraction in a glass prism.
Recall the seven visible-spectrum colours ordered by frequency and wavelength.
Know that single-frequency visible light is monochromatic.
Study of light and its behaviour.
Study of how light reflects from surfaces.
Explain refraction, critical angle, internal reflection and total internal reflection, including refractive index, equations and optical-fibre applications.
Explain converging and diverging lenses, define focal terms, construct ray diagrams, describe images, magnification and vision correction.
Explain prism dispersion, identify visible-spectrum colours by frequency and wavelength, and recognise monochromatic light.
Order the main electromagnetic-spectrum regions by frequency and wavelength.
Know that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same high vacuum speed.
Describe typical uses of radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma radiation.
Describe harmful effects of excessive microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma exposure.
Explain satellite communication using low-orbit and geostationary satellites.
Know communication systems using microwaves, radio waves and optical fibres.
Distinguish digital signals from analogue signals.
Know that sound can be transmitted digitally or in analogue form.
Explain digital signalling benefits, including faster transmission and longer range through regeneration.
Arrange the main electromagnetic-spectrum regions by frequency and by wavelength.
Know that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same very high speed in a vacuum.
Describe typical applications of radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma radiation.
Describe how excessive exposure to microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays can harm people.
Explain that artificial-satellite communication mainly uses microwaves, including low-orbit and geostationary satellite applications.
Know the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and approximately the same in air.
Explain how microwaves, radio waves and visible or infrared light support mobile, wireless, Bluetooth, cable television and broadband communication.
Distinguish between digital and analogue signals.
Know that sound may be transmitted using either digital or analogue signalling.
Explain that digital signalling enables faster data transmission and longer range through accurate regeneration.
Describe sound production by vibrating sources.
Describe sound as a longitudinal wave.
State human hearing as approximately 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Know that sound transmission requires a medium.
Know that sound travels through air at approximately 330–350 m/s.
Explain compressions and rarefactions.
Know that sound generally travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases.
Describe measuring distance and time to determine sound speed in air.
Explain how amplitude and frequency affect loudness and pitch.
Describe an echo as reflected sound.
Define ultrasound as sound above 20 kHz.
Describe ultrasound uses in material testing, medical scanning and sonar, including distance calculations.
Explain that vibrating sources produce sound.
Describe sound waves as longitudinal waves.
State that human hearing typically covers frequencies from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Know that sound requires a medium for transmission.
State that sound travels through air at approximately 330–350 m/s.
Determine sound speed in air by measuring distance travelled and travel time.
Relate sound amplitude to loudness and frequency to pitch.
Describe an echo as sound waves reflected from a surface.
Define ultrasound as sound having a frequency above 20 kHz.
Describe sound compressions and rarefactions.
Compare sound speeds, noting that sound generally travels fastest in solids and slowest in gases.
Describe ultrasound applications in material testing, medical imaging and sonar, including distance calculations.
Explain that sound is produced by vibrating sources.
State that human hearing typically spans frequencies from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Recognise that sound needs a medium for transmission.
Determine sound speed in air by measuring a distance and the corresponding travel time.
Describe an echo as sound produced by reflected sound waves.
Describe compressions and rarefactions in sound waves.
State that sound generally travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases.
Describe ultrasound applications in material testing, medical scanning and sonar, including distance calculations.
Describe forces between magnetic poles and between magnets and magnetic materials.
Describe induced magnetism.
Compare temporary soft-iron magnets with permanent steel magnets.
Distinguish magnetic from non-magnetic materials.
Define a magnetic field as a region where a magnetic pole experiences force.
Draw magnetic-field patterns and directions around a bar magnet.
Define field direction as the force direction on a north pole.
Plot magnetic fields with compasses or iron filings and use a compass to find direction.
Describe uses of permanent magnets and electromagnets.
Explain magnetic forces as interactions between magnetic fields.
Describe attraction and repulsion between magnetic poles and magnets and magnetic materials, including magnetisation and pole terminology.
Describe how magnetism can be induced in materials.
Distinguish between magnetic and non-magnetic materials.
Describe a magnetic field as a region where a magnetic pole experiences a force.
Draw magnetic field lines and their directions around a bar magnet.
State that field direction is the force direction acting on a north pole at that location.
Explain how compasses or iron filings reveal magnetic field lines and how a compass finds field direction.
Describe applications of permanent magnets and electromagnets.
Relate magnetic field strength to the spacing of magnetic field lines.
Describe forces between magnetic poles and between magnets and magnetic materials, using terms such as attraction, repulsion and magnetisation.
Describe how magnetism can be induced in a material.
Distinguish temporary soft-iron magnets from permanent steel magnets by their properties.
Distinguish magnetic materials from non-magnetic materials.
Draw the field-line pattern and directions around a bar magnet.
State that magnetic-field direction is the force direction on a north pole placed at that point.
Explain how compasses or iron filings plot magnetic field lines and how a compass gives their direction.
Relate the strength of a magnetic field to the spacing of its field lines.
State that charge may be positive or negative.
Describe attraction and repulsion between like and unlike charges.
Describe experiments producing and detecting electrostatic charge by friction.
Explain frictional charging as transfer of electrons.
Describe an experiment distinguishing conductors from insulators.
Use an electron model to explain conductors and insulators, with examples.
State that charge is measured in coulombs.
Define an electric field as a region where charge experiences force.
Define electric-field direction as the force direction on a positive charge.
Describe electric-field patterns around charges, conducting spheres and oppositely charged parallel plates.
Know that electric current relates to the flow of charge.
Describe using analogue and digital ammeters with different ranges.
Explain metallic conduction as movement of free electrons.
Distinguish direct current from alternating current.
Define current as charge per unit time and use I = Q/t.
State that conventional current flows positive to negative, opposite to electron flow.
Define e.m.f. as work done per unit charge by a source around a complete circuit.
State that e.m.f. is measured in volts.
Define potential difference as work done per unit charge passing through a component.
State that potential difference is measured in volts.
Describe using analogue and digital voltmeters with different ranges.
Use the equation E = W/Q to calculate e.m.f.
Use the equation V = W/Q to calculate potential difference.
Use R = V/I to calculate resistance.
Determine resistance experimentally using voltmeter and ammeter measurements.
Describe how metallic-wire resistance depends qualitatively on length and cross-sectional area.
Sketch and explain current–voltage graphs for a resistor, filament lamp and diode.
Use that metallic resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area.
Explain that circuits transfer energy from sources through components to the surroundings.
Use P = IV to calculate electrical power.
Use E = IVt to calculate electrical energy.
Define the kilowatt-hour and calculate appliance costs using this energy unit.
Study electrical quantities, including charge, current, electromotive force, potential difference, resistance, energy and power.
Learn about positive and negative charge, electrostatic effects, charging by friction, electric fields, conductors and insulators.
Learn how current relates to charge flow, how ammeters are used, electron conduction in metals, and the difference between direct and alternating current.
Define e.m.f. and potential difference, state their units, use their equations, and describe how to measure potential difference with voltmeters.
Use the resistance equation, measure resistance experimentally, describe how wire dimensions affect resistance, and interpret current–voltage graphs.
Explain energy transfer in circuits, calculate electrical power and energy, and use kilowatt-hours to determine appliance running costs.
Draw and interpret circuits containing listed sources, controls, components and measuring instruments.
Draw and interpret circuits containing diodes and LEDs, including their behaviour.
State that current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.
Construct and use series and parallel circuits.
Calculate the combined e.m.f. of sources connected in series.
Calculate the combined resistance of resistors connected in series.
State that source current in parallel exceeds the current in each branch.
State that two parallel resistors have less combined resistance than either alone.
State the advantages of connecting lighting lamps in parallel.
Calculate junction currents, series potential differences and parallel potential differences.
Explain that currents entering and leaving a junction have equal totals.
Calculate the combined resistance of two resistors connected in parallel.
State that conductor potential difference increases with resistance at constant current.
Describe how a variable potential divider operates.
Use the potential-divider equation for two resistors.
Understand circuit components, circuit arrangements, their electrical behaviour, and safe operation.
Draw and interpret circuits containing common electrical components, including diodes and LEDs, and explain their behaviour.
Construct, use and analyse series and parallel circuits, including their currents, potential differences, electromotive forces and resistances.
Relate potential difference to resistance at constant current; describe variable potential dividers and use the two-resistor potential-divider equation.
State hazards from damaged insulation, overheated cables, dampness and overloaded mains connections.
Describe mains wires and explain why the switch belongs in the live wire.
Explain trip switches and fuses, selecting suitable ratings and settings.
Explain why appliance casings must be insulating or earthed.
State that a fuse protects double-insulated appliance wiring without an earth wire.
Identify mains electricity hazards; explain wiring, switches, fuses, trip switches, earthing and double insulation, including suitable protective settings.
Explain that motion across or changing magnetic linkage through a conductor induces e.m.f.
Describe an experiment demonstrating electromagnetic induction.
State factors affecting the magnitude of induced e.m.f.
State that induced e.m.f. opposes the change producing it.
Use the relative directions of force, magnetic field and induced current.
Describe a simple a.c. generator and the roles of slip rings and brushes.
Interpret e.m.f.–time graphs and relate features to generator-coil positions.
Describe magnetic-field patterns and directions around current-carrying wires and solenoids.
Experimentally identify magnetic-field patterns around straight wires and solenoids.
Explain relay and loudspeaker operation using current magnetism, with applications.
State qualitatively how field strength varies around wires and solenoids.
Describe field changes when current magnitude or direction changes.
Describe an experiment showing force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
Use the relative directions of force, field and current.
Determine force direction on charged-particle beams in magnetic fields.
Explain coil turning and how turns, current and field strength increase the effect.
Describe motor operation, including split-ring commutator and brushes.
Describe a simple soft-iron-core transformer.
Use primary, secondary, step-up and step-down terminology.
Use the transformer voltage–turns ratio.
Explain transformer operation using electromagnetic induction.
Describe transformers in high-voltage electricity transmission.
State advantages of transmitting electricity at high voltage.
Use the equation IpVp = IsVs for an ideal transformer.
Use P = I²R to explain reduced cable losses at higher voltage.
Understand electromagnetic effects involving currents, magnetic fields, induction and electrical machines.
Understand how changing magnetic fields or conductor motion induce electromotive force.
Understand how a.c. generators produce alternating electromotive force using rotating coils or magnets.
Understand the magnetic fields produced by currents and their applications in relays and loudspeakers.
Demonstrate and predict the force on current-carrying conductors and charged-particle beams in magnetic fields, including effects of reversing current or field.
Explain how a current-carrying coil turns in a magnetic field and how increased turns, current or field strength increase the turning effect; describe commutator operation.

Describe transformer construction and operation, use primary, secondary, step-up and step-down terminology, apply transformer equations, and explain high-voltage transmission and reduced cable losses.

topics.title: 5.1 The nuclear model of the atom

outcomes.text: Describe atoms as positive nuclei surrounded by orbiting negative electrons.
Explain positive and negative ion formation by electron loss or gain.
Explain how alpha scattering supports the nuclear model.
Describe nuclei as containing protons and neutrons.
State relative proton, neutron and electron charges as +1, 0 and −1.
Define proton and nucleon numbers and calculate neutron number.
Use nuclide notation.
Explain isotopes and state that elements can have multiple isotopes.
Describe nuclear fission and fusion, including qualitative mass and energy changes.
Relate proton number to nuclear charge.
Relate nucleon number to relative nuclear mass.
Understand that atomic structure is explained by a small, positively charged nucleus containing most mass, with electrons around it.
Describe atoms and ions, and explain how alpha-particle scattering supports the nuclear model.
Describe nuclear composition, charges, proton and nucleon numbers, isotopes, nuclide notation, fission and fusion.
Define background radiation.
Identify major background-radiation sources, including radon, rocks, food and cosmic rays.
State that ionising radiation is measured with a detector and counter.
Use count rates measured per second or per minute.
Use background measurements to calculate corrected count rate.
Describe nuclear radiation emission as spontaneous and random in direction.
Identify alpha, beta and gamma emissions by nature, ionisation and penetration.
Describe alpha, beta and gamma deflection in electric and magnetic fields.
Explain relative ionisation using kinetic energy and electric charge.
Describe radioactive decay as spontaneous, random change of an unstable nucleus.
State that alpha or beta decay produces a different element.
Explain why isotopes may be radioactive because of excess neutrons or excessive nuclear mass.
Describe how alpha, beta and gamma emissions alter nuclear stability and neutron excess.
Use nuclide equations for alpha, beta and gamma decay.
Define half-life and use it in simple calculations.
Determine half-life from data or decay curves without background subtraction.
Choose isotopes for applications using radiation type and half-life.
State effects of ionising radiation, including cell death, mutations and cancer.
Describe safe transport, use and storage of radioactive materials.
Explain radiation protection through shorter exposure, greater distance and shielding.
Understand radioactivity, including detecting nuclear emissions, the three emission types, radioactive decay, and half-life.
Understand background radiation, its sources, detection, count-rate measurement, and correction for background counts.
Identify alpha, beta and gamma emissions, comparing their nature, ionising effects, penetration, and deflection in electric and magnetic fields.
Explain radioactive decay as spontaneous, random nuclear change producing alpha, beta or gamma radiation; describe isotope causes, element changes, nuclear effects and decay equations.
Define and calculate half-life using data or decay curves, and explain isotope applications based on radiation type, half-life, penetration and absorption.
Understand radiation’s biological effects and safe handling, storage, transport, and exposure-reduction precautions.

topics.title: 6.1 The Earth and the Solar System

outcomes.text: Use Earth’s tilted daily rotation to explain apparent solar motion and day and night.
Use Earth’s annual orbit to explain seasonal cycles.
Use the Moon’s monthly orbit to explain its repeating phases.
Define average orbital speed and use v = 2πr/T.
Describe the Solar System’s Sun, planets, minor planets, moons and smaller bodies.
Compare rocky inner planets with large gaseous outer planets using accretion theory.
Explain accretion using gravity, interstellar material, rotation and disc formation.
State that planetary, minor-planet and comet orbits are generally elliptical with the Sun off-centre.
Analyse planetary data on orbit, density, temperature and surface gravitational field strength.
Understand Earth, the Moon, and the Solar System through their rotations, orbits, cycles, and orbital speed.
Explain Earth’s rotation, orbit around the Sun, the Moon’s orbit, resulting cycles, and calculate average orbital speed.
Relate a planet’s surface gravitational field to its mass and distance from the planet.
Describe the Sun as a medium-sized hydrogen-and-helium star emitting mainly infrared, visible and ultraviolet radiation.
Describe galaxies, the Milky Way, stellar distances and the light-year, including its approximate value in metres.
Describe the Sun as a medium-sized star, mainly hydrogen and helium, radiating energy as infrared, visible and ultraviolet radiation.
Explain that stable stars release energy through nuclear fusion, converting hydrogen into helium.
Describe galaxies, the Milky Way, stellar distances and the light-year as the distance light travels in one year.
Recall that one light-year is approximately 9.5 × 10¹⁵ metres.
Describe stellar evolution from interstellar cloud and protostar through stable star, giant stages and final remnants.
Describe the Milky Way as one of billions of galaxies and recall its approximate diameter of 100,000 light-years.
Describe the Sun as a medium-sized hydrogen-and-helium star emitting mainly infrared, visible and ultraviolet radiation.
Explain that stable stars produce energy by fusing hydrogen into helium through nuclear reactions.
State that galaxies contain billions of stars; the Sun belongs to the Milky Way; other stars are farther away; distances use light-years.
Recall that one light-year represents approximately 9.5 × 10¹⁵ metres.
Describe star formation, development into giants or supergiants, and possible endpoints including white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes.
